readme: Reviewed measure-kind mismatches for audit-unit-basis-outlier.ps1. A cell lands here when its size names a different KIND of quantity than its shelf-mates (a volume among weights, or the reverse) but the NUMBER is still right, so the published per-unit is correct. That is the ordinary case for products whose density is near water, and for pack sizes a store states in one unit and the capture converts to the other. Keyed on commodity + store + the exact SIZE STRING that was reviewed: change the size and the review is void and the guard speaks up again, which is what stops a blanket per-store silence. NEVER add an entry to make the guard green - the entry has to say why the NUMBER is right, not why the flag is annoying. A cell whose number is wrong is fixed with a commodity exclude or add-known-wrong.ps1, not here (butter's pancake syrup and baby-formula's ready-to-feed liquid were both fixed that way on 2026-08-08, not allowlisted).

allow.reason: The size string names a VOLUME (1 pt) on a weight-priced row, but the number behind it is already a weight: the cell's own basis reads 'size 11.2 oz', and 11.2 oz is the standard net weight of a retail pint clamshell of blueberries. $2.59 / 11.2 oz = 0.2313, which is the published 0.2312, so compare-deals did the conversion correctly and only the LABEL is volume-shaped. Cross-checked against the identical 1 pt -> 11.2 oz conversion on the same board at Family Fare ($3.99 = 0.3563) and Hy-Vee ($4.99 = 0.4455), neither of which holds the crown; Aldi being cheapest is consistent with its position across the rest of the board. Allowlisted because the NUMBER is right, not because the flag was inconvenient - had the pint been divided by 16 fl oz instead of 11.2 oz the cell would have understated blueberries by about 30% and this would have been a commodity exclude, not an entry here.
The can is 18.8 oz by WEIGHT - the product name says '18.8 OZ' - and the size field labelled the same number as fl oz. Same number either way, so the per-oz figure is correct.

The product name states its own arithmetic: 'Magnolia Sweetened Condensed Milk, 14 oz., 6 pk.' - 6 x 14 oz = 84, by WEIGHT, which is the unit condensed-milk is priced in. The size field carries the right number under the wrong label ('84 fl oz'). $11.98 / 84 oz = 0.1426, which is the published per-unit, so the conversion was done correctly and only the label is volume-shaped. Same shape as the clam-chowder and horseradish-sauce entries above: the NUMBER is right. Not an exclude, because the product IS sweetened condensed milk; had 84 been a genuine fluid measure the weight would be about 95 oz and the cell would have OVERSTATED the price, which is the safe direction and still not worth publishing.
A 32 fl oz water-based spray on a commodity priced per oz. Density is within a few percent of water, so fl oz and oz are interchangeable here at the precision the board publishes.

A 26 fl oz water-based trigger spray (Seventh Generation Disinfecting Spray) on a row priced per weight oz whose peers are net-weight aerosols (Lysol 12.5/19 oz, Great Value 19 oz, OdoBan 14.6 oz). Density is within a few percent of water, so 26 fl oz is about 27 oz and 5.19/26 = 0.1996 OVERSTATES the per-weight-oz price by about 4 percent, which is the safe direction for a crown-holder: an overstated cell cannot win a crown it has not earned. It beats the runner-up (Walmart 0.2511) by 20 percent, so the crown holds at any plausible density. Same shape and same argument as the 2026-08-08 entry for the same commodity at Baker's (Scrubbing Bubbles, 1 pk 32 fl oz), whose product commit b28788fa moved to shower-cleaner on 2026-09-06, which is what put this previously unreviewed size string on the crown. NOT an exclude: the product IS a disinfectant spray and its number is exact.
The product name states '12 oz' and the size field states '12 fl oz'. Same number, opposite label, so the per-unit is unaffected.

The size names a VOLUME on a weight-priced row, and the number behind it is the product's own: the item is 'Ortho Home Defense ... 1 gal.' and 1 US gallon is exactly 128 fl oz, so the capture converted the label correctly and only the KIND is volume-shaped. $15.99 / 128 = 0.1249, which is the published per-unit. The product is a water-based ready-to-use insecticide, density within a few percent of water, so 128 fl oz weighs about 133 oz - meaning the published 0.1249/oz OVERSTATES the true per-weight-ounce price by roughly 4%. That direction is what makes this safe to allow while it HOLDS THE CROWN: an overstated cell cannot win a crown it does not deserve, only lose one it does. Same shape and same argument as the disinfectant-spray entry above. Had the conversion gone the other way - a gallon divided as though it were 16 oz - the cell would have understated by 8x and this would have been a commodity exclude, not an entry here.

The row is priced per FL OZ and the size field labels its number 'oz', but the number is the product's own volume: the item states '200.2 Fl Oz' and the size carries 199.583 - a 0.3% difference, which is rounding in the capture's own conversion, not a different quantity. $14.37 / 199.583 = 0.0720, the published per-unit. Dividing by 199.583 rather than the stated 200.2 OVERSTATES the per-fl-oz price by 0.3%, the safe direction for a crown-holder. The NUMBER is right; only the label is weight-shaped.
The product name states '200.2 Fl Oz' and the size field states '200.303 oz'. The row is priced per fl oz; the two numbers agree to within 0.05%, so the label is the only thing that differs.

The size names a WEIGHT token on a row priced by volume, but 128 is the true fluid-ounce content: this is the gallon jug, and Fareway's own product page says so - the captured link ends /fareway-orange-juice-from-concentrate-128-oz. $5.98 / 128 fl oz = 0.046719, which is the published 0.0467, so the conversion was done correctly and only the label is weight-shaped. The price is a real markdown the row carries itself (base_price 9.99, current_price 5.98, marked_down true), not a parse artifact. Cross-checked against the gallon peers on the same board, all of which price the identical 128 fl oz volume: Aldi $7.49 = 0.0585, Baker's 1 gal $8.79 = 0.0687, Hy-Vee 1 gal $8.99 = 0.0702. Fareway is cheapest because it is the only one on ad this week. Had 128 been misread for a 64 fl oz bottle the cell would read 0.0934 and OVERSTATE orange juice by double, so the failure direction was checked, not assumed. Allowlisted because the NUMBER is right; the bare 'oz' token on a liquid is ordinary retail shorthand and appears the same way on this store's other juice rows.
Mt. Olive 1 gal. One gallon is 128 fl oz and pickle brine is near water, so 126.8 oz is a faithful weight conversion of the stated gallon rather than a basis error.
Member's Mark 1 gal. Ranch dressing runs about 1.06 g/ml, so 128 fl oz is roughly 135.7 oz by weight - 135.25 is a faithful conversion of the stated gallon, not a mismeasure.

A 16 oz bottle of Our Family red wine vinegar on a row priced per fl oz. Vinegar is about 95% water and its density is within about 1% of water, and 16 is the same number whichever unit the shelf tag names - the standard retail bottle is 16 fl oz and Family Fare's own tag writes it '16 oz'. $2.49 / 16 = 0.1556, the published per-unit, so the arithmetic is right and only the KIND label is weight-shaped. Same class as the clam-chowder entry above: one number, two labels. If anything the ~1% density difference overstates the per-fl-oz price, which cannot hand this cell a crown it has not earned.

The size names a VOLUME on a row the guard scored as weight, but the row's OWN declared unit is floz per the commodity rule file, so this is the one cell on the row whose label matches the divisor compare-deals used. 2.48 / 15 fl oz = 0.16533, the published 0.1653, taken verbatim from walmart-regular-2026-08-31.json (current_price 2.48, size 15 fl oz). The flag exists because 4 of 6 sized peers label their bottles by net weight oz, which flipped the peer majority from 3-3 to 2-4 when Baker's cell changed from Subway Sweet Onion (16 fl oz) to Kikkoman Gochujang (21.5 oz) on 09-02; the same crown was green on 08-30 and 08-31, re-run hermetically to prove it. Crown checked for robustness both ways across the whole plausible density range 1.00 to 1.16 oz-weight per fl oz: per weight-oz Walmart is 0.1425 to 0.1653 against Sam's Club 0.1738, and per fl oz Walmart is 0.1653 against Sam's Club 0.1738 to 0.2017. Walmart is cheapest at every point, so no published verdict changes. Same shape and same argument as the pickles at Sam's Club 126.8 oz entry of 2026-08-08. NOT an exclude, because the product IS teriyaki sauce and its number is exact.
